{{More citations needed|date=August 2025}}

'''Algebraic-group factorization algorithms''' are algorithms for [[Integer factorization|factoring an integer]] ''N'' by working in an [[algebraic group]] defined [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] ''N'' whose group structure is the direct sum of the 'reduced groups' obtained by performing the equations defining the group arithmetic modulo the unknown prime factors ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ''p''<sub>2</sub>, ...  By the [[Chinese remainder theorem]], arithmetic modulo ''N'' corresponds to arithmetic in all the reduced groups simultaneously.

The aim is to find an element which is not the identity of the group modulo ''N'', but is the identity modulo one of the factors, so a method for recognising such ''one-sided identities'' is required. In general, one finds them by performing operations that move elements around and leave the identities in the reduced groups unchanged. Once the algorithm finds a one-sided identity all future terms will also be one-sided identities, so checking periodically suffices.

== Algorithm ==
Computation proceeds by picking an arbitrary element ''x'' of the group modulo ''N'' and computing a large and [[smooth number|smooth]] multiple ''Ax'' of it; if the order of at least one but not all of the reduced groups is a divisor of A, this yields a factorisation. It need not be a prime factorisation, as the element might be an identity in more than one of the reduced groups.

Generally, A is taken as a product of all the prime powers below some limit B<sub>1</sub>, and ''Ax'' is computed by successive multiplication of ''x'' by these primes; after each multiplication, or every few multiplications, the check is made for a one-sided identity. (A less efficient naive version would use a product of all integers below the limit B<sub>1</sub>.)<ref name=Galbraith>{{cite book |last1=Galbraith |first1=Steven |title=Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=261-268 |url=https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~sgal018/crypto-book/ch12.pdf |access-date=16 August 2025 |chapter=Primality Testing and Integer Factorisation using Algebraic Groups}}</ref>

=== The two-step procedure ===
It is often possible to multiply a group element by several small integers more quickly than by their product, generally by difference-based methods: one calculates differences between consecutive primes and adds consecutively by the <math>d_i r</math>. This means that a two-step procedure becomes sensible, first computing ''Ax'' by multiplying ''x'' by all the primes below a limit B<sub>1</sub>, and then examining ''p Ax'' for all the primes between B<sub>1</sub> and a larger limit B<sub>2</sub>. This would relax the smoothness requirement for the group order from being B<sub>1</sub>-powersmooth to being the product of a prime between B<sub>1</sub> and B<sub>2</sub> and a B<sub>1</sub>-powersmooth number.

The difference-based method is the basic "stage 2" method. There exist modifications such as [[Peter Montgomery (mathematician)|Montgomery]]'s prime pairing (1978) and the Brent-Suyama extension.<ref name=MontgomeryKruppa08>{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=Peter L. |last2=Kruppa |first2=Alexander |title=Improved Stage 2 to P ± 1 Factoring Algorithms |journal=Algorithmic Number Theory |date=2008 |volume=5011 |pages=180–195 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-79456-1_12 |url=https://inria.hal.science/inria-00188192/file/pm1fft-final.pdf}}</ref>

A more efficient "stage 2" method uses polynomial multiplication implemented via [[fast Fourier transform]]. This method was originally demonstrated for Lenstra's ECM by Montgomery in 1992,<ref name=PZ06>{{cite journal |last1=Zimmermann |first1=Paul |last2=Dodson |first2=Bruce |title=20 Years of ECM |journal=Algorithmic Number Theory |date=2006 |volume=4076 |pages=525–542 |doi=10.1007/11792086_37|url=https://members.loria.fr/PZimmermann/papers/ecm-submitted.pdf}} [https://inria.hal.science/inria-00070192v2 HAL]</ref> but has since been adapted for ''p''-1 and ''p''+1.<ref name=MontgomeryKruppa08>{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=Peter L. |last2=Kruppa |first2=Alexander |title=Improved Stage 2 to P ± 1 Factoring Algorithms |journal=Algorithmic Number Theory |date=2008 |volume=5011 |pages=180–195 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-79456-1_12 |url=https://inria.hal.science/inria-00188192/file/pm1fft-final.pdf}}</ref>

== Methods corresponding to particular algebraic groups ==

=== Practical methods ===
If the algebraic group is the [[multiplicative group]] mod ''N'', the one-sided identities are recognised by computing [[greatest common divisor]]s with ''N'', and the result is the [[Pollard's p-1 algorithm|''p''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 method]].

If the algebraic group is the multiplicative group of a quadratic extension of ''N'', the result is the [[Williams' p + 1 algorithm|''p''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 method]]; the calculation involves pairs of numbers modulo ''N''.  It is not possible to tell whether <math>\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z [ \sqrt t]</math> is actually a quadratic extension of <math>\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z </math> without knowing the factorisation of ''N''. This requires knowing whether ''t'' is a [[quadratic residue]] modulo ''N'', and there are no known methods for doing this without knowledge of the factorisation. However, provided ''N'' does not have a very large number of factors, in which case another method should be used first, picking random ''t'' (or rather picking ''A'' with ''t'' = ''A''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;4) will accidentally hit a quadratic non-residue fairly quickly. If ''t'' is a quadratic residue, the p+1 method degenerates to a slower form of the ''p''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 method.

If the algebraic group is an [[elliptic curve]], the one-sided identities can be recognised by failure of [[inverse function|inversion]] in the elliptic-curve point addition procedure, and the result is the [[elliptic curve method]]; [[Hasse's theorem on elliptic curves|Hasse's theorem]] states that the number of points on an elliptic curve modulo ''p'' is always within <math>2 \sqrt p</math> of ''p''.

All three of the above algebraic groups are used by the GMP-ECM package,<ref>{{cite web |title=ZIMMERMANN Paul/ecm (GMP-ECM) |url=https://gitlab.inria.fr/zimmerma/ecm |website=gitlab.inria.fr}}</ref> which includes efficient implementations of the two-stage procedure, and an implementation of the PRAC group-exponentiation algorithm which is rather more efficient than the standard [[binary exponentiation]] approach.

=== Other groups ===
The use of other algebraic groups—higher-order extensions of ''N'' or groups corresponding to algebraic curves of higher genus—is occasionally proposed, but almost always impractical. For example, one can use the [[Jacobian variety]] of a [[hyperelliptic curve]], which has an efficient group law. These methods end up with smoothness constraints on numbers of the order of ''p''<sup>''d''</sup> for some ''d''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, which are much less likely to be smooth than numbers of the order of ''p''.{{Citation needed|date=February 2026}}

== Practical considerations ==

=== Complexity ===
The naive first stage uses <math>O(B_1 \log (B_1) M(\log (N)))</math> bit operations, while the prime-powers-only first stage takes <math>O(B_1 M(\log (N)))</math>, with ''N'' being the number-to-be-factored and <math>M(x)</math> denoting the cost of multiplying two ''x''-bit integers (practically <math>M(\log (N)) = O(N \log (N) \log \log (N))</math> using FFT-based methods).<ref name=Galbraith/>

The standard (difference-based) second stage uses <math>O((B_2 - B_1) M (\log (N)) )</math> bit operations.<ref name=Galbraith/> The polynomial-based second stage uses <math>O(\sqrt{B_2- B_1} \log (B_2- B_1) M(\log (N)))</math> bit operations (the <math>B_1</math> term can be discarded assuming <math>B_2 >> B_1</math>, which is often the case). Varying the size of the convolution gives a trade-off between memory and space: for each doubling of memory usage, double the amount of advancement in <math>B_2</math> can be made for the same amount of computation.<ref name=MontgomeryKruppa08/>

=== Probability of success ===
See Kruppa (2010) sections 5.3 and 5.4.<ref name=Kruppa>{{cite thesis|url=https://docnum.univ-lorraine.fr/public/SCD_T_2010_0054_KRUPPA.pdf|date=2010|title=Speeding up Integer Multiplication and Factorization|last=Kruppa|first=Alexander|degree=PhD|publisher=Henri Poincaré University}} &ndash; Work describes algorithms that Kruppa had contributed to GMP-ECM and other factoring programs. Some chapters have been published elsewhere.</ref>
